advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Stop the diagnostic probe from reparenting the child to the same target the mutation-under-test writes (use a throwaway/third parent or a non-mutating probe, or reset the field) so the round-trip oracle observes only set_parent's effect.
evidence: `dc_request` is `conftest._request`, which performs a real HTTP PUT: `req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=body, method=method)` / `urllib.request.urlopen(req, ...)` (tests/external/live_jira_dc/conftest.py:98-109)

probe wiring reparents to the same target as the mutation under test: `probe_status, probe_body = _probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, child, second)` and `_probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, child, second, verb="update")` at test_dc_mutations.py:1392-1395 (inbound) and 1702-1705 (outbound), both BEFORE `dc_transport.set_parent(child, second)` at :1403 / :1714

no reset between probe and mutation-under-test, and the outbound oracle then reads the field back and accepts second: `_assert_remote_parent_is(child, status, body, second, previous_parent=first, ...)` (test_dc_mutations.py:1717-1723) — value could originate from the probe
ticket AC1 seeks to observe whether set_parent's write moves the parent; a probe that itself moves the parent to the same value invalidates that observation (rebar:1a9f-50c0-e7a5-4fda AC criteria)
advisory.finding: The diagnostic probe issues a REAL live PUT reparenting the child to `second` — the identical target the mutation-under-test `set_parent(child, second)` writes — BEFORE that mutation and with no reset, so if DC accepts the probe's write the round-trip oracle passes on the probe's effect rather than set_parent's, producing a false green that masks the silent-no-op regression these cells exist to catch.
scenarios: DC 8.17.1 accepts a raw sub-task fields.parent (or update-verb) PUT and actually moves the parent: the probe reparents child->second, set_parent is a no-op, but both oracles read second and pass green
advisory.suggested_fix: Probe against a distinct throwaway parent (or a non-effecting target) and/or re-read + reset fields.parent to `first` after the probe, before calling set_parent — so the post-mutation oracle attributes the parent value solely to set_parent.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Have the probe (or its caller) re-read fields.parent after the PUT and fold the read-back into the diagnostics so a 2xx accept-and-ignore is distinguishable from a write that landed.
evidence: probe returns only the PUT response: `return dc_request(f"/rest/api/2/issue/{key}", method="PUT", payload=payload)` (_dc_support.py:602) with no follow-up field read

ticket AC1 method requires the read-back: 'issue a direct PUT fields.parent and capture (status, body), then re-read fields.parent. A 2xx with an unchanged read-back is accept-and-ignore; a 4xx is rejection.' (rebar:1a9f-50c0-e7a5-4fda comment)

diagnostics string only reports the PUT status/body, not a post-PUT parent read: `f"raw PUT (fields form) for the reparent -> HTTP {probe_status}, body {str(probe_body)[:300]}..."` (test_dc_mutations.py:1396-1401)
advisory.finding: The probe captures the PUT's (status, body) but never re-reads fields.parent after it, so it cannot distinguish the ticket's AC1 cases ('a 2xx with an UNCHANGED read-back is accept-and-ignore; a 4xx is rejection') — a 2xx probe alone is ambiguous, weakening the diagnostic below what AC1 specifies.
scenarios: DC returns 200/204 for the raw PUT but ignores it: the folded diagnostic shows only '2xx' with no read-back, so a CI reader cannot tell accept-and-ignore from a write that landed

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the reparent probe target a throwaway parent (or a clearing PUT) rather than `second`, or reset the child's parent back to `first` after probing, so the diagnostic PUTs cannot pre-apply the mutation the oracle attributes to `dc_transport.set_parent`.
evidence: test_dc_mutations.py:1392-1395: `probe_status, probe_body = _probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, child, second)` then `_probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, child, second, verb="update")` — both target `second`, the same destination as the mutation under test
test_dc_mutations.py:1403 `dc_transport.set_parent(child, second)` runs AFTER the three probe PUTs, with no intervening reset of the parent back to `first`

_dc_support.py:597-602: the probe's `fields`-form payload `{"fields": {"parent": {"key": new_parent}}}` is the identical shape `set_parent` sends (docstring: 'sends the SAME shape set_parent sends'), so a probe that DC honors performs the reparent the test means to attribute to set_parent
_dc_support.py:494 `assert_remote_parent_is`: passes as soon as `got == expected_parent`, verifying only final state, not which write produced it
ABSENCE: the precondition asserting the child starts under `first` (test_dc_mutations.py:1693 / :1378) runs BEFORE the probes, so it cannot detect that a probe already moved the child to `second`
advisory.finding: In both reparent tests, `_probe_subtask_parent_put(dc_request, child, second)` (and its `verb="update"` twin) issues a real `PUT fields.parent -> second` — the exact mutation and destination the test's own oracle later checks for — BEFORE `dc_transport.set_parent(child, second)` runs, with no parent reset in between. The oracle asserts only the final observable state (`fields.parent == second` / local `parent_id == second_local`), so if DC ever actually applies the PUT (bug fixed, or different DC behavior), the diagnostic probe pre-applies the mutation under test and a broken `set_parent` would still make the oracle pass. This is regression blindness introduced into the test's core assertion.
scenarios: DC 8.17.1 (or a fixed/patched instance) actually applies `PUT fields.parent`, so the probe reparents child->second and the oracle passes regardless of set_parent's correctness
A future regression breaks `dc_transport.set_parent` for sub-tasks while DC honors raw PUTs — the test stays green because the probe already did the reparent
advisory.suggested_fix: Point the probe PUTs at a third seeded parent (or `new_parent=None` clear) distinct from `second`, and re-assert/restore the child is under `first` immediately before calling `dc_transport.set_parent(child, second)`, so the oracle's transition first->second is attributable solely to set_parent.
